What's the actual difference between the 3 grades of fuel. I've only ever used unleaded, but what is the point of the other two?

The three grades that you speak of are all unleaded. The difference will be octane and additives. Additives will vary by brand. A higher octane means that the fuel will be compressed more before it ignites. Some engines call for a specific octane rating, use that. Modern cars are more forgiving of using the wrong octane and will adjust accordingly to reduce/eliminate knocking.
Don't most cars just take the low grade? That's all I've ever used. Never knew to even look up what kind my car should use.

Most, yes. It depends on what the engine was designed for. An engine with a turbo will probably call for a higher octane. A highly tuned engine will probably call for an higher octane. It is in the manual that came with the car.

To expand on what the other guy said, in a gas engine you don't want the fuel-air to ignite until the spark goes off at just the right moment of the stroke. However, fuel-air will spontaneously explode under pressure (this is how diesel engines operate), and as the piston comes up it compresses the fuel-air all the way to the top of the stroke when the spark ignites it. If a low octane fuel is used in a higher compression engine it can detonate too early, which will make bad noises and put severe stresses on the mechanics, as well as rob power by pushing down on the cylinder while it's still on the up stroke. Most turbo and tuned engines run higher compression and will have a sticker or something around the gas cap that says 'minimum octane rating 91' for instance. You might get away with 89, but 83 could cause problems. Also higher octane and compression leads to more efficient fuel burn, so at 89 you will notice a reduction in power and miles per gallon, even if with no serious problems.

A higher octane means that the fuel will be compressed more before it ignites. Some engines call for a specific octane rating, use that.

I bet you already know this, but you didn't explain it very well. Engines with higher compression ratios squeeze the fuel/air more to get more power out of the same amount of gas, but low octane gas will explode on its own when it's squeezed too tight. Some cars are made to run on regular, at the cost of some performance and vice versa. All engines have a minimum octane rating at some level.

Articles online state that you neednt let a gas engine warm up in the winter time, that even in -30c you can turn over the engine and start driving, (obviously this doesn't apply to diesel engines) what's your take on that?

The strain of pulling the pistons down against 18-20 inches of engine vacuum is quite a bit greater than driving gently (this is partly why diesels are more efficient, they don't have any intake manifold vacuum). The purpose of a warmup is this- an engine is composed of different types of metals, for example cast iron and aluminum. Those have a different rate of thermal expansion. You need to slowly let the engine warm up, otherwise one will expand faster and cause damage. Let's say you have an iron block with aluminum heads. That's common.
